title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 33-40
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 33-40 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: In an agent framework, what does the Runner own?
options: The loop that drives the run to a final answer
The retry logic for failed provider requests
The persistence of history across separate runs
The scoring of answers against a golden set
questions.explanation: The Runner owns the reason-act-observe loop: it calls the model, runs any requested tools, feeds results back, and repeats until the model returns a final answer.

questions.question: What does declaring a structured output type give an agent's result?
options: A shorter reply that saves output tokens
A typed object that downstream systems can consume
A reply already checked for factual accuracy before sending
A faster reply that skips prose generation entirely
questions.explanation: A structured output turns a free-form reply into a typed data contract that downstream systems can read fields from directly.

questions.question: A tool the agent can call hits a bad input. Why return a readable error string instead of raising?
options: Raising hides the failure from the monitoring layer
Raising makes the tool slower to call on the next turn of the run
Raising ends the run, while a readable string lets it recover
Raising lets the tool skip its own input validation
questions.explanation: An enterprise tool that raises crashes the whole run, so it returns an error message the model can read and act on instead.

questions.question: A run is expected to take well past ten seconds. What feedback does the user need?
options: A progress indicator that sets expectations and a way to interrupt
A percentage bar that counts down the remaining work one step at a time
The model's raw reasoning streamed continuously to the user
No feedback at all, since the latency is unavoidable here
questions.explanation: Past the ten-second attention limit, the user needs a progress indicator that says what to expect plus a way to interrupt the run.

questions.question: An agent UI runs two signals, the answer and the work. How should they be used?
options: Stream the answer only, keeping the work hidden from the user
Report the work only, so the answer can appear all at once
Report the work for reassurance and stream the answer for tolerability
Render both signals at token granularity so a step list builds from tokens
questions.explanation: The two signals do different jobs: the answer streams at token granularity to make the wait tolerable, while the work is reported per completed item to reassure the user.

questions.question: Why prefer a step list over a percentage bar for an agent run?
options: A step list uses fewer tokens than a percentage bar
An agent has no fixed step count, so any percentage would be faked
A step list lets the model's private reasoning become the visible steps
A percentage bar cannot be updated while the run is in progress
questions.explanation: Because the loop has no fixed step count, a percentage would be invented, so naming each completed unit of work is honest and useful.

questions.question: Why derive each chunk's ID deterministically from its source instead of using a random UUID?
options: So a change or delete event can locate its vectors without a full scan
So the vector store can compress the index far more efficiently over time
So the embedding model returns more accurate vectors for each chunk
So duplicate documents are removed automatically during retrieval
questions.explanation: A random ID has no link back to its source, so a delete or change cannot find the affected vectors; a deterministic ID turns every later operation from a scan into a lookup.

questions.question: An update arrives and the pipeline embeds it and adds it to the index. Why is that a bug?
options: The new chunk will be embedded with the wrong model version entirely
The index will re-embed every unchanged chunk as well
The update is lost because its ID collides on insert
The old stale chunk stays retrievable, so the model sees both
questions.explanation: Adding a new vector for the same item leaves the old chunk retrievable, so the retriever returns both and the model sees contradictions; the fix is to upsert on a stable ID.

questions.question: Why must changing the embedding model trigger a re-embed of the corpus?
options: A new model always produces vectors with a different number of dimensions than before
Vectors from different models live in incompatible spaces and cannot be mixed
The old vectors become unreadable once the model is retired
Re-embedding is required to refresh each document's content hash
questions.explanation: Different embedding models place vectors in incompatible spaces, so queries and documents must be embedded by the same model; any model change forces a re-embed even when dimensions match.

questions.question: Agent output is stochastic. What testing approach does that call for?
options: Assert exact output strings and fail the build whenever any of them change
Skip automated testing entirely, since no two runs ever match
Test the properties of outputs and the deterministic layers around it
Review every run by hand before release
questions.explanation: The model is a moving target, so you pin down the deterministic layers with assertions and score the fuzzy end with an evaluator kept honest by a frozen baseline.

questions.question: What distinguishes an integration test of an agent from a unit test?
options: It scores real model output with an LLM judge against a golden set
It runs the whole loop against controlled tool side effects
It measures the cost per request under sustained production load
It stubs the model and asserts only on a prompt string
questions.explanation: An integration test runs the real loop with mocked tools that return fixed data, so it can assert on tool selection, arguments, ordering, and that nothing destructive ran.

questions.question: Why must a regression golden set stay frozen?
options: So the evaluator does not start agreeing with whatever the model does
So its cases stay small enough to run on every single commit cheaply
So it can be refreshed automatically from live production traffic over time
So the same cases can double as integration tests
questions.explanation: Refreshing the baseline from production data teaches the evaluator to bless the current model's output instead of judging correctness, which is eval contamination.

questions.question: Why does an agent break the assumption behind conventional CI/CD?
options: Its behavior is shaped by code, model, prompts, and data at once
Its full test suite takes too long to run on every commit
Its dependencies cannot be pinned inside a build artifact
Its behavior is fully determined by application code alone and never changes
questions.explanation: An agent's behavior is shaped by the model, the prompts, and the retrieved data as well as the code, and any of them can change without a single line of application code changing.

questions.question: How should a canary release of a new prompt behave for a conversational agent?
options: Compare the canary against a historical monthly baseline and redeploy to roll back
Route each request independently so traffic mixes freely between both versions
Split a small slice of traffic and compare the two versions against each other
Wait for full rollout before scoring any quality metric from the canary
questions.explanation: The canary and the stable version run concurrently and are compared with each other, rollback is an instant routing change rather than a redeploy, and conversational agents are pinned by session.

questions.question: What does pinning a model registry version in the build give you?
options: A guarantee that the provider will never change the model version underneath you
A reproducible artifact, so a week-old build behaves as it did when tested
A replacement for the evaluation dataset as evidence of quality
An automatic rewrite of prompts when their quality drifts
questions.explanation: Pinning the model registry version, each prompt revision, and the provider API version makes the build reproducible, so an old artifact still behaves as it did when it was tested.

questions.question: At scale, how should observability be understood?
options: As a decision system where metrics, alerts, and SLOs play a role
As a viewing window where a human reads every trace by hand, one by one
As a monthly cost report produced at the end of each month
As a replacement for running production evals on every commit
questions.explanation: At scale the trace stops being the primary interface and becomes evidence you open after a metric or alert tells you where to look; the metrics, alerts, dashboards, and SLOs make the decisions.

questions.question: Which three metric groups does an agent need, beyond plain service health?
options: Latency, throughput, and error saturation budgets
Operational, economic, and quality proxy
Trace, span, and log
Input, output, and cache
questions.explanation: Operational metrics track whether the system works, economic metrics track what it costs, and quality proxy metrics like retry and refusal rate lead a bad answer before an eval runs.

questions.question: Why is uptime not the same as reliability for an agent?
options: Because agents cannot emit a standard error rate metric
Because agent latency thresholds differ from a web service's in every way
Because an agent can be fast, up, and returning a 200 while it is wrong
Because agents are monitored with different observability tools
questions.explanation: A traditional service fails by being slow, down, or erroring, but an agent can be perfectly healthy operationally while producing the wrong answer or exposing sensitive data.

questions.question: You open one failing trace. In what order should you check it?
options: Repeated tool calls, then a mismatched tool result, then climbing input tokens
Infrastructure metrics first, then a service restart, and only then the failing trace
Context length first, then prompt wording, and then the tool schemas
A historical baseline first, then the alert history, and then the trace
questions.explanation: Repetition in the trace means a loop, a tool result that does not match its stated success means a bad tool, and input tokens climbing turn over turn mean context bloat; the first yes names the class.

questions.question: How is a loop best defined?
options: Any run that calls a given tool more than once during the same run
The same decision made twice with no new information between them
Any run that simply exceeds its framework step cap
Any run that retries after a tool returns an error message
questions.explanation: A loop is the same decision made twice with no new information between the two, which excludes an agent that tries three genuinely different queries.

questions.question: A tool returns HTTP 200 with an empty body and no error flag. What is the right fix?
options: Raise the framework step cap so the agent can retry more
Log the empty result and continue on without ever changing the tool
Mark the result as an error and return an actionable message
Truncate the tool's output so it uses fewer tokens
questions.explanation: A tool that cannot do its job must say so with a truthful error status and a message the model can act on, because the caller is a model that will otherwise take the empty result as the answer.

questions.question: What is the central framing of a support agent?
options: Mostly a routing problem with a retrieval step and a capped action boundary
A free-running agent that decides everything dynamically
A reasoning problem whose success depends on the model's raw reasoning capability
A system that must fully automate every case to be worth building
questions.explanation: A support agent is mostly a routing problem with a retrieval step in the middle and a hard limit on what it may do, and most production failures come from getting one of those three wrong.

questions.question: How should the common, well-defined support intents be handled?
options: Hand the whole conversation to a free-running agent
Route the classified intent into a constrained, predetermined path
Build a separate free-running agent per intent
Let the retrieval step decide the path with no separate routing pass
questions.explanation: Common intents are well-defined tasks with a known end state, so they belong in predictable workflow paths, while open-ended agent behavior is reserved for the unstructured long tail.

questions.question: How should the tool boundary be drawn for a support agent?
options: Give the agent both read and write tools to keep the whole design simple
Keep write tools in the prompt so the model gates its own actions
Let the agent hold the billing credentials so it can act directly
Default every tool to read-only and add write tools under guard
questions.explanation: Starting read-only caps the blast radius: a tool that returns order status is safe to deploy broadly, while a tool that writes or refunds is added only behind its own policy check.
